candidates.title: Large language model developments
candidates.abstract: Abstract Large language models (LLMs) are generative artificial intelligence (AI) models trained with vast amounts of data and context, and excel at processing, understanding and generating human language, using transformer models to learn statistical relationships between tokens. LLMs are a subset of transformer models, and hence are closely related but not interchangeable. Given the ‘explosion’ of LLM research, the challenge is tracking emerging developments and matching LLMs to applications. This paper reviews LLM developments with the aim of understanding the underlying models’ computational strengths and weaknesses, building on previous work focusing on LLM optimization (Sharkey & Treleaven 2025 Optimising large language models: taxonomy and techniques. SSRN Scholarly Paper no. 5278456. Rochester, NY: SSRN). We find that despite their power, LLMs (transformers) face several key challenges. These include: (i) computational complexity and resource requirements—training and deploying large models is extremely costly and slow, and energy consumption is a concern; (ii) understanding long sequences and dependencies—even with enhancements, models can struggle with very long-range dependencies or context lengths beyond their window (e.g. maintaining coherence in a long document), which reflects the more fundamental absence of continual learning; (iii) interpretability and bias—it remains difficult to interpret why a model produces a given output, and models can inadvertently amplify biases present in training data; and (iv) optimization challenges, including fine-tuning for specific tasks without overfitting or losing generality and ensuring efficient inference (latency, the delay before a response is completed) for real-time applications. In summary, this review focuses on architectural, optimization and interpretability developments in LLMs. It does not aim to provide a systematic benchmark comparison, exhaustive implementation details or empirical performance evaluation, which are covered extensively elsewhere. The authors are committed to updating this review aligned to constant changes in the technology; please reach out with any additions.

candidates.title: Secure Domain Adaptation and Retrieval Augmented Generation for Compact Language Models Using Archived Cybersecurity Intelligence
candidates.abstract: Abstract Security analysts must reconcile vulnerability, exploit and malware records that are scattered across public repositories, yet it is unclear whether compact, locally deployable language models can reason over such archives. We present SecureLLM, an open framework that normalizes 161,190 records from the National Vulnerability Database, the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog, ExploitDB and MalwareBazaar into one corpus, which we use both to continue pretraining Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct and to build a dense retrieval index. We compare the adapted model with its base and three other compact models on 1,000 stratified security prompts, with and without retrieval (10,000 responses), using paired non-parametric tests. Continued pretraining lowered validation loss by 12% during training but left cybersecurity-term coverage in closed-book answers statistically unchanged (Holm-adjusted p = 0.062). With retrieval, the adapted model's answers agreed less with the retrieved context than those of its base (cosine similarity 0.41 versus 0.46; adjusted p < 0.001). On a balanced 10,000-sample EMBER malware test set, gradient-boosted trees reached 0.856 accuracy, whereas the zero-shot language models reached 0.646 (base) and 0.630 (adapted), with precision near 0.91 but recall of only 0.32 and 0.29. In a 100-sample pilot, adding retrieved-neighbor statistics to the prompt made the model label every sample benign. We trace these outcomes to four causes: a mismatch between raw-text pretraining and instruction-style use, a mismatch between the prompt set and the corpus, encoder truncation, and uninformative retrieval neighborhoods. We release the pipeline and propose a leakage-controlled evaluation protocol for cyber-intelligence language models.

candidates.title: Naming the deliverable raises convention coverage in large language model outputs
candidates.abstract: Abstract Practitioners compress conventions into a name such as RACI matrix or term sheet, whereas outsiders can only describe the deliverable. We tested whether the name matters when large language models write professional deliverables. Each request had three versions differing in one phrase, the practitioner name or one of two lay descriptions. Blind model judges scored outputs against convention checklists from public normative sources. On 40 curated terms, the name raised convention coverage in all six models, by 0.11 [95% CI 0.07, 0.16] to 0.29 [0.22, 0.37], and the gain survived masking the name, rebuilt checklists, and length control. On 150 terms sampled by rule from O*NET and Wikidata, it replicated in four models (0.11 [0.08, 0.14] to 0.19 [0.16, 0.23]) and was largest for method names. Gains were largest in models with the lowest lay coverage, a pattern confounded with vendor and output length. On curated terms, log-probabilities from an open model correlated moderately with per-term gains (ρ = 0.37). Using a name obtained from the model recovered about half to three quarters of the gain, mostly when the name was correct. We propose knowing that deliverables have names, asking for them, and checking them as an AI-literacy skill.

candidates.title: Origami as a Spatial and Geometric Reasoning Benchmark
candidates.abstract: Multimodal language models perform well on visual recognition and on tool use, but these abilities do not transfer directly to spatial and geometric reasoning. Geometric structure does not reduce to text or to a single image: exact angles and incidences, which surface lies in front of which, and the order in which operations were applied are not recoverable from a semantic description of a scene. We introduce CP2Seq, a benchmark for evaluating geometric reasoning and sequential planning in multimodal language models through origami. The benchmark contains 600 procedurally generated samples, each requiring a model to produce a valid sequence of folds from a crease pattern and a target folded state. Samples are produced by a deterministic folding engine. Ground truth is recorded during generation. We release the generation and evaluation framework to support additional samples and experiments across reference depths and action models. During evaluation, the engine executes proposed folds or rejects invalid actions with explicit feedback, while the model remains responsible for selecting actions and searching for a solution. We evaluate multimodal language models under progressively greater tool assistance, and against a deterministic breadth-first search over the same action set. Candidate sequences are assessed by executing them and comparing the resulting folded state with the target, allowing for planar translations, rotations, and reflections. Performance falls off sharply with sequence depth: in the Luna ablations no configuration solves a medium or hard sample (11 or more folds), while some-layers solves rise from 6/30 to 18/30 with higher reasoning effort. Failures are dominated by search rather than by illegal moves: in the broader evaluation, 48% of episodes end by revisiting earlier states. A breadth-first search over the same actions, under its own time budget, solves 54.7% of easy-group attempts, so short sequences are within reach of systematic search.

candidates.title: Unifying and Beyond the Theory of Pervasive Capability Degradation in LLM Post-training SFT from Feature Interference
candidates.abstract: Pervasive Capability Degradation (PCD) refers to the phenomenon in which supervised fine-tuning (SFT), while adapting a large language model (LLM) to a target task, often erodes the general capabilities acquired during pre-training. Prevailing explanations attribute PCD to macroscopic distribution shift and therefore lack microscopic manipulability, leaving existing mitigation methods without a complete theoretical foundation. In this paper, we first develop a bottom-up geometric theory of PCD grounded in feature interference under superposition: narrow-domain SFT data disrupt the almost-orthogonal feature structure formed during pre-training, and the resulting interference drives activations across decision hyperplanes in the output Laguerre-Voronoi geometry, flipping predictions on general tasks. This theory unifies existing methods into six paradigms and reveals both the source of their efficacy and their theoretical limits. We then prove that cross-entropy under one-hot supervision cannot resolve PCD on its own, and accordingly propose the AEGIS loss, which directly constrains the drift of activation margins along all competing token directions, thereby decoupling interference suppression from task adaptation. Across 3 model families and 14 SFT tasks, AEGIS outperforms representative methods of every paradigm on target tasks and pervasive capabilities simultaneously, at only about 1.3 times the computational cost of standard SFT. Its generality, scalability, and mechanistic interpretability offer a new perspective on fully resolving PCD.

candidates.title: Feeling of Knowing in Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Post-training updates change what large language models (LLMs) can answer, but may leave their answerability judgments misaligned. We study this knowledge-judgment desynchronization through functional feeling of knowing (FoK), which supports selective generation, retrieval triggering, and model routing without implying subjective experience. We propose two trainable channels: a knowledge channel that changes answerability and a FoK channel that judges the current knowledge state. Three stages train them: on-policy supervised fine-tuning (OP-SFT) updates knowledge from corrected on-policy answers; knowledge-delta FoK training (K$Δ$-FT) adapts judgments across intermediate knowledge states; and FoK-guided policy optimization (FGPO) trains the subsequent answer or explanation. Factual-QA experiments, cross-dataset evaluation, and three sequential updates show that explicit FoK alignment improves judgment quality on updated knowledge. MMLU and ARC-Easy separately assess capability preservation.

candidates.title: Reliability Stress Testing of RAG Retrieval under Query-Relevant Corpus Poisoning
candidates.abstract: External text can affect a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) system only after the retriever admits it to the model context. We stress this admission step while varying document content, attacker query information, per-target poison budget, and contamination scope. Across 623 Benchmarking Information Retrieval (BEIR) queries from SciFact and NFCorpus, five query-targeted documents per query reduce classical-retriever nDCG@10 by 40.2-61.5% in isolated-target stress. Full-query anchoring explains most Best Matching 25 (BM25) degradation, whereas appended text also shifts latent semantic analysis (LSA) and Hybrid rankings. A pretrained BGE-small validation reaches 100% target exposure for query-only P=5 on both datasets; adding the injection payload changes SciFact nDCG only from 0.269 to 0.271 and lowers NFCorpus exposure slightly to 98.8%, indicating that query anchoring remains the dominant retrieval-side factor for this dense model. Query length materially changes the interpretation of partial-information attacks: on 162 long SciFact queries, two random terms cover 19.9% of eligible terms and still yield 39.5% Hybrid target exposure. Multi-target contamination adds cross-target interference. Overlap-based admission can remove full-query poisons but may sharply reduce clean retrieval utility, and maximal marginal relevance (MMR) leaves exposure unchanged under the tested configuration. The study measures retrieval-layer failures, not downstream instruction following.

candidates.title: OperAItor: An Agentic Framework for Fault-Tolerant Operation of Chemical Processes
candidates.abstract: OperAItor, an open-source framework for developing and evaluating large language model agents for supervisory fault management in chemical processes. The framework is demonstrated on a dynamic reactor-distillation process representing isopropanol dehydrogenation, with physically based thermodynamics and modified reaction kinetics to permit liquid-phase operation. The process is represented by a 113-variable differential-algebraic model and operates at a nominal feed rate of 100kmol/h, producing approximately 4t/h of acetone. The simulated plant includes 8 PI control loops, 22 process alarms, 5 duty-standby pump trains, and 11 independent safety instrumented functions. The agent architecture integrates multivariate statistical process monitoring, fault diagnosis, knowledge-graph retrieval, action planning, and supervisory action generation. Five action-validation configurations are investigated, comprising operation without validation, an LLM-based judge, digital-twin simulation, and deterministic admissibility checks with and without consequence projection. The framework is evaluated using four LLMs across 20 scenarios involving single and multiple simultaneous faults. Without agent intervention, 18 scenarios result in plant stops, corresponding to an economic loss of $399,000 relative to fault-free operation under the assumed benchmark economics. For GPT-5 nano, Qwen3 8B, and Mistral 7B, validated agent configurations reduce the number of stops to 5-8 and recover $265,000 of the loss. The study provides a reproducible benchmark for comparing agent architectures, language models, and action-validation methods for supervisory fault management in chemical processes.

candidates.title: Narrative Factor Extraction Using Large Language Models and Its Implications for Asset Pricing
candidates.abstract: Drawing on Shiller's theory of narrative economics, this article puts forward the "narrative-sentiment-pricing" (NSP) transmission mechanism and divides the transmission process from narrative to asset pricing asset pricing into three stages, namely narrative germination, sentiment diffusion and expectation solidification. Then, through non-diversifiability and heterogeneity relative to classical factors, it is argued that the narrative constitutes an independent source of systematic risk. At the factor construction level, this paper proposes a narrative factor (NARR) extraction method based on large language models (LLMs). At the level of asset pricing testing, this paper designs three testing paths. Incorporate NARR into the Fama-French multi-factor model for incremental information testing; place NARR under Merton's ICAPM framework to distinguish between rational hedging demand and behavioral deviations; and finally, introduce NARR into the stochastic discount factor (SDF) framework for a no-arbitrage test. The above paths jointly build a complete evaluation system to verify the independent pricing power of narrative factors, and also provide practical reference for subsequent empirical research on narrative factors.

candidates.title: LatentTriad: Pre-Action Risk Representations for Malicious Agent Skill Detection
candidates.abstract: Large language model agents are increasingly extended with reusable skills, but untrusted skill content can induce operations outside the user's task. Detecting this contextual risk requires more than suspicious-pattern matching, while dynamic analysis incurs the cost of skill execution. We find that hidden states formed during prefill contain readable information about task-operation consistency, including across held-out expression forms in controlled evaluations. Matched Operation-state interventions also affect later Boundary states and shift fixed risk readouts toward the donor label. Based on these findings, we introduce LatentTriad, which combines contextual Boundary features, group-adjusted Operation directions, and departures from benign state relationships. All branches share one prefill: detection generates no output tokens, invokes no tools, and executes no skill code. Across 5,830 skill packages from five sources and seven backbones, LatentTriad achieves 99.0-99.2% pooled F1 and 93.0-94.6% source-macro F1. A separately measured compact implementation completes prefill and detection in a median of 259-284 ms. These results connect pre-action risk readability and functional influence to execution-free skill screening.

candidates.title: Large Language Models for Forecasting of Electricity Price Spikes
candidates.abstract: Can market notices read by a large language model (LLM) improve short-horizon electricity price spike forecasts? We study five regions of Australia's National Electricity Market. A local LLM extracted features once per notice, only notices visible at the forecast origin were used, and a gradient-boosting model produced onset probabilities. In an out-of-sample development back-test (July 2022 to July 2024), notice features did not lower the 60-minute Brier score of a numeric model including the market operator's next-hour forecasts. At 24 hours they did, but rule-based features did so almost equally and attribution to notice content was not established. A locally frozen protocol, not publicly deposited, governed a retrospective single-use holdout from 15 August to 17 October 2026. At 60 minutes, the hypothesis that LLM features lower the numeric model's Brier score was not established (H1; relative Brier skill -0.09%), so the planned comparison with rule-based features was not tested (H2). At 24 hours, the hypothesis that LLM features lower the score against a text-free control was not established (H3; +0.37%, 95% CI [-9.74, 1.39], inconclusive). By the frozen wording rule the non-significant 24-hour improvement comes mainly from recalibration and cannot be attributed to notice content, although post hoc the decomposition could not separate recalibration from resolution. The 24-hour base rate was 1.56% on the holdout against 14.0% in development. With 5 onsets on 3 days and 24-hour positives in 2 of 22 three-day blocks, the holdout neither established nor excluded a 24-hour effect.

candidates.title: Large Language Models for Automated Web-Form-Test Generation: An Empirical Study—RCR Report
candidates.abstract: This report presents a framework that enables the reproduction and extension of our empirical evaluations using Large Language Models (LLMs) for automated web-form-test generation. The framework includes HTML pruning , context construction , prompt design , LLM communication , and web-form-test insertion . It involves the construction of three types of prompts (from HTML) to guide the test generation: Raw HTML for Task Prompt (RH-P); LLM-Processed HTML for Task Prompt (LH-P); and Parser-Processed HTML for Task Prompt (PH-P). The framework provides an LLM communication module that standardizes interactions with provider APIs. Our study utilized public-API models and demonstrated that PH-P consistently achieved a higher successfully submitted rate (SSR) than RH-P and LH-P. To support the replication of our work, we have released the source code, a dataset subset, and the relevant scripts.

candidates.title: Large Language Model-Assisted Adaptive Heuristic Search for Agile Earth Observation Satellite Scheduling
candidates.abstract: Agile Earth observation satellites must coordinate imaging tasks within limited observation windows, while accounting for attitude maneuvering and onboard energy constraints. Competition among observation opportunities makes scheduling performance sensitive to the heuristic rules used for task selection. This letter proposes a large language model (LLM)-assisted adaptive heuristic search method for agile Earth observation satellite scheduling. The LLM generates an initial heuristic rule according to the characteristics of the scheduling instance. During the subsequent ant colony search, search performance and scheduling information are fed back to the LLM to refine the heuristic rule. The proposed modifications are evaluated through paired solution constructions before being incorporated into the search process. A unified scheduling procedure determines task selection, satellite assignment, and observation timing under the operational constraints. Experiments on six scheduling scenarios involving 50--200 imaging tasks demonstrate that the proposed method achieves 4.3\%--9.6\% higher mean observation benefit than the strongest baseline.

candidates.title: Generation of Case-Based Materials Using Large Language Models in Health Professions Education: Scoping Review
candidates.abstract: Abstract Background Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to generate case-based materials for health professions education (HPE). Previous reviews have examined broad applications in HPE or focused on clinical cases, but none have comprehensively synthesized the generation and evaluation of diverse case-based materials. Objective This study aims to synthesize current evidence on LLM-generated case-based materials in HPE, focusing on generation approaches, evaluation methods, key findings, and reported challenges. Methods This scoping review followed the Joanna Briggs Institute methodology and PRISMA-ScR (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews) reporting guidelines. Seven databases (PubMed, Embase, Scopus, Web of Science, CINAHL, ERIC, and IEEE Xplore) were searched on May 10, 2026, for studies published from January 1, 2017. Eligible studies were peer-reviewed original research articles, published in English, reporting the use of generative LLMs to create text-based case-based materials for HPE. Data were synthesized using descriptive statistics and narrative synthesis. Results Seventy-two studies were included. Most were published between 2024 and 2026 (67/72, 93%) and focused on medical education (59/72, 82%), with undergraduate students as the most frequently studied population. Case-based multiple-choice questions (MCQs; 28/72, 39%) and clinical cases or vignettes (22/72, 30%) were the most frequently generated materials. Generative Pretrained Transformer-4 (GPT-4) family models were the most commonly used (40/72, 55%), and generation predominantly relied on relatively simple prompting approaches, whereas more advanced strategies, such as few-shot prompting, prompt chaining, or use of external knowledge sources, were rarely adopted. Evaluation primarily relied on expert review, typically involving small panels, while student assessment (25/72, 35%) and psychometric analyses were less common. Overall, LLM-generated materials were frequently judged to be clinically plausible, structurally clear, and reasonably aligned with educational objectives, particularly after refinement. However, consistent limitations included factual inaccuracies, construction flaws, superficial clinical realism, pedagogical misalignment, suboptimal psychometric performance, and bias. No LLM consistently outperformed others, although methodological heterogeneity limits cross-study comparisons. Conclusions This review provides a comprehensive synthesis of the literature on LLM-generated case-based materials in HPE. Unlike previous reviews examining broad educational applications or focusing on clinical cases, it integrates evidence across a broad range of case-based materials while synthesizing generation methods, evaluation approaches, reported findings, and challenges. The evidence suggests that LLMs can support the development of case-based materials but still require expert oversight because of recurring concerns regarding clinical accuracy, educational quality, psychometric performance, clinical realism, and bias. By identifying methodological and evidence gaps, this review provides educators, curriculum developers, and researchers with a structured overview of this rapidly evolving field and may inform the development of more robust generation workflows, more standardized evaluation approaches, and the responsible use of LLM-generated case-based materials in HPE.

candidates.title: FourSight: Stable FP4 RL Post-Training via Sequence Filtering and Sparse Channel Compensation
candidates.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) post-training increasingly targets low-bit deployment, with NVFP4 weight-and activation quantization (W4A4) becoming the state-of-the-practice format. However, integrating NVFP4 into RL degrades rollout quality and amplifies cross-engine training-inference mismatch (TIM), destabilizing training. We show that these failures are concentrated rather than uniform - severely mismatched tail tokens concentrate in a few outlier sequences, while policy weights remain largely intact and quantization error concentrates in a few high-variance activation channels. Guided by this, we present FourSight, an algorithm-system co-design with two targeted solutions: TIM-aware sequence filtering that excludes drifted trajectories from policy updates, and sparse precision compensation that keeps only top-variance channels in BF16 while retaining native NVFP4 elsewhere. We further design a fused SpliceGEMM kernel with specialized prefill and decode datapaths to minimize overhead. FourSight sustains near-BF16 accuracy and strong FP4 deployment quality across models and engines, while improving step-to-accuracy by 1.76-2.60x and staying within 2.3% of FP4 step time up to 120B-scale models.

candidates.title: Collaborative Search Meets Large Language Models: An Empirical Study
candidates.abstract: Collaborative search enables users to address complex information needs jointly. Advances in large language models (LLMs) enable autonomous agents to support collaborative information seeking within shared communication spaces. However, little is known about how these agents shape search experiences, behaviors, and outcomes compared with conventional search tools. We conduct a user study with 80 students working in 40 pairs. Each pair completes four collaborative search tasks under four scenarios: QAAgent, which answers queries using an LLM's parametric knowledge; CoSearchAgent, which uses multi-user conversational context to reformulate queries, retrieve web information, and generate source-grounded answers, while asking clarifying questions when needed; an in-chat search plugin that returns result lists; and manual Google Search. After each task, participants complete several questionnaires assessing their search experience and independently write a report; after all tasks, they participate in individual interviews. Results show that LLM-based agents reduce perceived workload, support collaboration, and reshape communication and evidence-use practices. They also encourage more independent paraphrasing, albeit at the cost of report richness. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first systematic empirical comparison of LLM-based agents and conventional tools for collaborative search across search experience, user behavior, and collaborative outcomes.

candidates.title: Aligning Training and Rollout Policies for End-to-End FP4 RL on Mixture-of-Experts LLMs
candidates.abstract: In this work, we study end-to-end FP4 reinforcement learning (RL) post-training for Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) large language models. Recent work on FP4 RL has introduced effective recovery recipes that restore accuracy under aggressive low-precision quantization for dense models, but we find that the same approach yields no improvement over the naive FP4 baseline in the MoE setting. We conduct an in-depth study to understand why. Our analysis identifies the root cause in the routing mechanism unique to MoE: because the router makes discrete expert-selection decisions, training-inference policy alignment becomes acutely sensitive to whether the same recovery technique is applied symmetrically on the training and inference sides. When an asymmetric recipe is used-including the dense-model approach, which corrects only the rollout-training-inference alignment deteriorates sharply, as measured by the Pearson correlation coefficient between training and inference probabilities, and router selection matching rates. Building on this finding, we propose MoeResQ, a quantization-recovery recipe for MoE RL post-training that enforces symmetry between the training- and inference-side corrections. MoeResQ restores training-inference alignment and substantially closes the accuracy gap to full precision, establishing symmetric recovery as the key principle in FP4 RL for MoE models.

candidates.title: AdSteer: Native Advertising in Large Language Model Generation
candidates.abstract: Large language model (LLM) services face rapidly rising serving costs. To sustain free or affordable access for a broad user base, alternative monetization mechanisms are needed. Native advertising offers a promising approach, as it creates economic value by aligning user intent with merchant offerings. Yet how to integrate sponsored content naturally into LLM responses remains largely underexplored. Existing approaches primarily rely on prompt-level injection, multi-pass rewriting, or fine-tuning, which can compromise response quality or introduce additional computational costs. We propose AdSteer, a lightweight decoding-time advertising framework that adaptively adjusts token probabilities to integrate contextually appropriate advertisement into responses. AdSteer calibrates the strength and duration of advertising influence, making sponsored content a natural part of the response. Experiments on GEM-Bench across three application scenarios show that AdSteer achieves an average improvement of 14.1% in overall score over the strongest baselines and 22.5% fewer total tokens on average than rewrite-based methods. These results demonstrate that AdSteer provides an effective and practical solution for native advertising in LLMs.

candidates.title: TraceRouter++: Causal Semantic Routing Realignment via Optimal Transport
candidates.abstract: Despite their remarkable capabilities, large foundation models (LFMs) remain susceptible to adversarial manipulation. Current safety intervention methods primarily rely on the \textit{locality hypothesis}, rigidly suppressing isolated neurons or features. However, harmful semantics manifest as distributed, cross-layer circuits, rendering localized ablations both brittle against complex jailbreaks and detrimental to general utility. To bridge this gap, we propose TraceRouter++, a routing-level safety intervention framework that explicitly traces safety-relevant causal routing pathways activated under harmful inputs and realigns their unsafe activation states. Our framework operates in a \textit{Discover-Trace-Realign} paradigm: it first pinpoints a sensitive onset layer via attention divergence and disentangles dense activations into interpretable routing features using sparse autoencoders (SAEs). Subsequently, it maps these features to downstream causal circuits via feature influence scores (FIS). Crucially, departing from rigid suppression paradigms, TraceRouter++ introduces a constrained optimal transport (OT)-based soft routing realignment. By formulating safety intervention as a tractable coordinate-wise marginal optimal transport approximation, our method redirects unsafe activation marginals toward safe-reference marginals within causally identified routing subspaces while preserving non-selected coordinates at the intervention point. This mechanism safely redirects malicious semantic flows while leaving orthogonal computational routes intact. Extensive experiments across representative large language models (LLMs), multimodal large language models (MLLMs), and diffusion models (DMs) show that TraceRouter++ outperforms evaluated baselines, improving adversarial robustness while maintaining a favorable safety-utility trade-off. candidates.title: ToolSpace: Scaling Tool-Centric Environment Synthesis for Long-Horizon Agents
candidates.abstract: Large language models are deployed as long-horizon agents that compose diverse tools across MCP services into executable workflows. Existing MCP environment-scaling methods are data-centric: they first synthesize a database and scenario, then derive tools and tasks from them. As a result, tool interfaces may not match real ones, tool compositions are not grounded in execution, and tasks rarely span more than one environment. We propose ToolSpace, a tool-centric framework that reverses this order. ToolSpace mines data, state, and retry dependencies from adjacent calls in execution traces of real MCP services and open agent corpora, using deterministic rules rather than LLM judgment, and clusters the resulting weighted tool-composition graph into environments. Databases are synthesized only for state-mutating environments, while query and stateless tools replay recorded returns. ToolSpace then performs state-aware random walks with rollback and decompiles each chain into a natural-language task with assertion-based checks, keeping only samples that replay successfully from the initial state. Applied to AutomationBench and tau3-Bench Banking, the pipeline produces harder Pro versions on which 7 frontier models drop by up to 38.2 points. Across seven long-horizon tool-use benchmarks, ToolSpace raises Qwen3.6-35B-A3B from 23.0 to 41.0 average score (43.2 with RL) and GLM-5.2 from 44.6 to 56.6, on par with Claude Opus 5. Ablations show that execution-witnessed edges clearly outperform LLM-judged ones, and performance keeps improving with data and environment scale.

candidates.title: Factorized MLLM Embeddings for Composed Image Retrieval
candidates.abstract: Composed Image Retrieval (CIR) aims to retrieve a target image given a reference image and a modification text. Although recent approaches leveraging Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have shown significant progress, we argue that the MLLM's compositional understanding remains underutilized. This stems from directly mapping composed queries into a retrieval embedding via contrastive supervision alone, without explicitly resolving the intended visual modifications. In this work, we introduce Factorized MLLM Embeddings (FactEmbed), which decouples compositional query comprehension from building discriminative embeddings. Rather than directly projecting the composed query into a single embedding without internal reasoning, FactEmbed employs a set of factorized latents that simulate the intended visual modifications via an intermediate target imagination objective. This process encourages the latents to ground into target semantics before forming discriminative representations for retrieval. Subsequently, to propagate these factorized representations throughout the model for retrieval, we optimize a factor-level contrastive loss while distilling the decomposed representations into a deeper attention layer of the MLLM. Finally, for efficient inference, we retain the [EOS] token to establish a global-level embedding on top of these factorized latents, while we exploit the mean-pooled factorized latents to rerank a short candidate list at negligible cost, as both are produced by the same forward pass. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that FactEmbed outperforms prior works across CIR benchmarks.

candidates.title: You don't need long context

We further demonstrate that LLM performance does not collapse on long-horizon software engineering tasks even when taking at most one action per context, and based on that we outline the concept of semantic state space models (SSSMs). Our findings question the need for long-context language models.

candidates.title: QueryFlow: Multi-Hop Graph Retrieval with Adaptive Query Evolution
candidates.abstract: Multi-hop retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) supports Web information seeking and fact verification by recovering complementary evidence across related pages within a limited retrieval budget. Scoring evidence independently against the original question can miss supporting units whose relevance emerges through intermediate facts. Iterative retrieval incorporates these facts into subsequent queries, while graph retrieval explicitly models relations among evidence units. Yet fixed-query graph retrievers update entity representations without adapting the query condition to accumulated relational context. We view multi-hop evidence recovery as the coupled evolution of evidence representations and query conditions, with accumulated context informing both what the retriever represents and how it searches for complementary evidence. QueryFlow realizes this perspective by recurrently integrating query-conditioned summaries of graph context into a shared query state, which controls boundary inputs and relation features for subsequent propagation. Across four representative multi-hop question answering (QA) datasets, QueryFlow achieves macro Recall@10 (R@10), Full Recall@10 (FR@10), and LLM-Acc gains of 4.98, 8.40, and 8.0 percentage points over representative baselines, respectively.

candidates.title: MaskRet-Oto: Region-Conditioned Evidence Retrieval and Calibration for Otoscopic Image Classification and Selective Referral
candidates.abstract: Abstract Digital otoscopy is a compact biomedical imaging modality, but retrospective image-classification results can be distorted by duplicate content, acquisition-domain cues, uncertain confidence, and dataset prevalence. We revised the framework as MaskRet-Oto, a region-conditioned evidence-retrieval and calibration pipeline rather than a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) system. The working archive contained 3,000 RGB otoscopic images in five approximately balanced categories. Exact-hash auditing identified 78 duplicated files; the remaining 2,922 images formed 1,956 within-class perceptual-hash groups that were kept intact across training (n=2,046), validation (n=438), and test (n=438) partitions. Because patient identifiers were unavailable, this procedure controls only exact/near-duplicate image leakage and cannot establish patient-independent evaluation; different views from the same patient or examination could remain in different splits. The soft central field-of-view operator retained 70.9% of image support and is now described as a predefined region-conditioning prior, not as empirical proof that shortcut learning was prevented. On the internal image-level test set, the compact 64 x 64 CNN pipeline achieved 98.17% accuracy (95% bootstrap confidence interval 96.80-99.32%), 98.23% macro-F1, MCC 0.977, and macro-AUC 0.9994. Training-only visual retrieval reached 99.54% top-5 recall. The source-tagged textual memory contains 15 curated statements retrieved by TF-IDF; no language model is used and the component is not presented as a clinical knowledge base or RAG. Retrieval fusion did not improve top-1 accuracy; its role is limited to exposing similar training cases, attaching source-tagged evidence, and contributing a small additional calibration change after temperature scaling. Selective prediction concentrated all observed errors in the lowest-confidence deciles in this same test set, but this is a post hoc internal utility surrogate, not a clinical-utility validation. The nearly balanced benchmark distribution also means that calibration values should not be interpreted as real-world disease-risk probabilities. Patient-level, device-diverse, prevalence-aware, and prospective validation with stronger standard backbones is required before clinical use.

candidates.title: HERIT: Enabling Global Access to Hanja-to-English Historical Translation by Mitigating Temporal Bias

This approach substantially expands the training dataset, mitigating both data scarcity and temporal overfitting across different historical periods. Extensive automated and human evaluations demonstrate that HERIT consistently outperforms baselines. Finally, we translate previously untranslated portions of the archives using our model, thereby enabling global access to these resources for researchers.

candidates.title: Who is the Pronoun Pro? Comparing LLMs and Humans at Number-Disambiguation of 'they'
candidates.abstract: This study evaluates whether large language models (LLMs) can reliably replace or complement human research assistants in linguistically complex annotation. In a controlled annotation task, 73 human annotators (local students and crowdworkers with and without a background in linguistics) and more than 40 LLM configurations number-disambiguated 174 authentic uses of 'they' from Reddit, including innovative and context-sensitive cases. The best LLM, Kimi K3, reached 94.5% accuracy, above the human majority vote (86.2%) and the mean of the top half of human annotators (78.5%); only the single best human annotator scored higher (95.7%). LLMs also offer substantial practical advantages in cost and speed. However, qualitative error analysis reveals a crucial complementarity: human reasoning in low-agreement cases exposes inconsistencies in the annotation typology and thereby improves the methodological framework itself. The study contributes (i) a benchmark-style human-LLM comparison for a semantically demanding task, (ii) transparent cost and time evidence, and (iii) a methodological argument against a purely replacement-oriented view of automation. LLMs are viable for large-scale annotation support in linguistics, but their responsible use requires human critical oversight. The dataset with its gold-standard labels, all human and LLM annotations, and the fully reproducible code are openly available as a Quarto-based, public repository.

candidates.title: When the Consumer Is an Agent: Execution-Grounded Service-Level Agreements
candidates.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly act as service consumers. They select operations and report whether a task is complete. In an asynchronous distributed service, an accepted call or immediate state read does not establish that the required state became observable by its deadline. An independent control plane observes a deadline-bound service-state predicate, admits completion, and directs recovery while the agent performs the task. We evaluate placement and deletion in a live multi-provider data service with heterogeneous models and an injected transfer delay. Across policies, some tasks that missed the deadline were accepted and some that met it were rejected. Under enforcement, accepted completions remained consistent with later observations; all included healthy tasks completed, and unresolved faulted tasks terminated as unverified. The results show that completion of these tasks can be governed by independent observation of service state rather than by the agent's self-assessment.

candidates.title: When Ground Truth Is Not Ground Truth: Automatic Labeling for Hallucination Detection
candidates.abstract: Hallucinations in Large Language Models (LLMs) remain a major challenge, as they can produce misleading, factually incorrect, or unverifiable information, thereby undermining their trustworthiness and reliability. However, reliable ground-truth labels remain a key challenge in evaluating hallucination detectors. Recent studies often construct labels automatically by comparing model generations with reference answers using similarity metrics such as BLEURT. This implicitly treats BLEURT similarity as a proxy for hallucination, despite its English-centric supervision, unbounded score range, and design as a similarity metric rather than a factuality measure, making threshold-based ground-truth construction potentially unreliable. Through comprehensive experiments using 15 automatic supervision judges, seven hallucination detection baselines, two generator models, two QA datasets, and five languages, we demonstrate that detector performance varies substantially with the choice of supervision judge. Human validation reveals substantial differences in labeling reliability, with QGen-9B achieving the lowest overall misclassification rate (12.86%), while BLEURT and BLEURT-n exhibit rates of 47.23% and 47.32%, respectively. Our findings highlight the limitations of automatic similarity-based labeling and the need for more reliable judging methods that better capture semantic and factual correctness.

candidates.title: What Does the Model See? Representation Validity in Multimodal LLM-Based Video Analysis

candidates.title: What Does 4-Bit Microscaling Cost a Wearable Activity Recognizer?
candidates.abstract: Wearable sports sensors can recognize actions on the device itself, where lower-precision numbers reduce model storage and memory traffic. Two 4-bit block-scaled formats, MXFP4 from the Open Compute Project, introduced in 2023, and NVFP4 from NVIDIA, introduced in 2025, are drawing interest. Published evaluations cover general deep-learning benchmarks and large language models; to our knowledge, nobody has yet measured what they cost a small wearable-sensor model. We train a 159,492-parameter 1D CNN to recognize four basketball actions from wrist-accelerometer data in Hang-Time HAR and test it on players it has never seen, using five-fold cross-validation grouped by player. Every comparison between number formats is made fold by fold. In full precision the model reaches 69.26\% macro-F1. Measured TFLite FP16 and INT8 models lose at most 0.16 percentage points. In simulation, 4-bit weights cost 1.45 points with MXFP4 and 0.72 points with NVFP4. When activations are quantized to 4 bits as well, MXFP4 loses 5.14 points and NVFP4 only 0.75, and NVFP4 comes out ahead in all five held-out-player folds. The ranking survives two alternative simulator settings, with NVFP4 leading by 3.49 to 4.40 points. A $2 \times 3$ ablation with 4-bit weights and activations (two block sizes and three scale rules) points to scale selection as the main source of MXFP4's loss. The reference MXFP4 conversion we simulate rounds the scale down, which can pick scales that are too small, so many blocks clip their largest values. Rounding the scale up recovers 3.18 points with 32-value blocks and 3.63 points with 16-value blocks, and switching to an 8-bit floating-point scale, as NVFP4 does, adds another 0.84 and 1.20 points. Block size matters less. Under this round-down rule, 16-value blocks score 0.44 points below 32-value blocks in all five folds; under the other two rules there is no consistent effect.

candidates.title: Validation-Gated ML Pipeline Synthesis with Expert-Grounded Self-Evolving Skills
candidates.abstract: Recent advances in large language models have enabled agentic systems that automate machine learning pipeline construction from minimal user input. However, existing agentic AutoML methods either depend on rigid templates that limit adaptability, target narrow task domains, or rely on free-form code generation that lacks reliability guarantees, leaving intermediate errors to propagate silently and degrade the final model. We present EvoML, an agentic framework for end-to-end ML pipeline synthesis built on expert-grounded skills that evolve across runs, executed through a validation-gated harness. The framework decomposes pipeline construction into four phases coordinated by three agents: an Orchestrator that enforces validation gates, advancing each phase only when its outputs pass structural, execution, and semantic checks, which precludes error propagation and keeps every artifact auditable; an Executor that runs expert-grounded skills, grounded in the nnU-Net workflow and pairing reusable templates with online adaptation; and a Curator that performs post-run evolution, consolidating the scripts and guidance recovered during a run into the skill library so it improves across datasets. We evaluate EvoML on eight datasets spanning six sophisticated, real-world ML task types, against agentic AutoML systems and command-line coding tools. EvoML achieves full automation and the best final model quality on all eight, spanning segmentation (up to 0.94 Dice), classification (0.99 accuracy), reconstruction (0.95 SSIM), and denoising (0.79 normalized PSNR), while transferring to broader ML tasks.

candidates.title: Training Specialist LLMs on Your Phone: Forward-Only Optimization via Block-Spectral Coordinates
candidates.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) on personal devices keep user data local, but limited memory restricts their general capability. Since most user-specific tasks do not require the breadth of frontier models, a practical solution is to adapt a shared on-device model into lightweight specialists. However, backpropagation is prohibitive in memory, and users rarely provide labeled data. We present MobileSpec, a system that trains specialists with forward passes alone and learns from automatically checked task outcomes, as in reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR). Because forward-only updates are built from random perturbations, training is efficient only when these perturbations resemble the weight changes of RLVR, which largely preserve the singular values of pretrained weights and rotate their singular vectors. The core algorithm of MobileSpec, FuRA-S, produces such perturbations while training only the block-spectral coordinates of pretrained weights, namely the singular values of their column blocks. As we show theoretically and empirically, rescaling these blocks independently shifts their relative contributions to each weight matrix and thereby rotates its singular vectors. Since this update can be rewritten as a transformation of the layer input, FuRA-S also adapts INT4 models without modifying their weights. With specialists of only 1-5 MB that update 0.015-0.05% of the parameters, MobileSpec raises the success rate of a phone-use agent from 6-23% up to 89-100% and trains a personalized 8B model on an iPhone 16 Pro overnight. On RLVR benchmarks, FuRA-S is competitive with full-parameter evolution strategies (ES) and outperforms ES over LoRA adapters and quantized ES on INT4 models.

candidates.title: Theoretical Analysis of Muon on Transformers for Next-Token Prediction
candidates.abstract: Muon has recently shown strong empirical performance in training Transformer-based large language models (LLMs), yet its optimization dynamics remain poorly understood from a theoretical perspective. In this paper, we analyze the training dynamics of Muon for next-token prediction (NTP) in Transformers. The training procedure consists of two phases: the preprocessing phase learns the output-value component, while the main phase learns the key-query component. For the preprocessing phase, we characterize the optimization trajectory exactly and show that the normalized spectral margin is optimal after each update. For the main phase, we establish nonasymptotic convergence rates for the training loss and the normalized margin gap under softmax attention. These results suggest that Muon's update rule can help models efficiently learn which tokens matter for prediction, offering a possible explanation for its strong performance in large language model training. The learned weight structure also yields a generalization guarantee for unseen contexts. Furthermore, we validate our theoretical insights with experiments on next-token prediction tasks.

candidates.title: The Right Source Is Not Enough: Understanding History Interference in Speech-LLM Memory
candidates.abstract: Speech large language models retain audio history to support multi-turn conversations. Yet remembering an event does not ensure that its information is used only when relevant. We investigate why irrelevant historical audio changes answers even when the queried event remains represented. Controlled experiments on MOSS-Audio and MiMo-Audio show that historical values direct errors toward specific competing answers, beyond a generic effect of context length. Causal interventions distinguish two paths. In open-ended question answering, most history-value errors disappear when subsequent computation cannot directly access the irrelevant source. In multiple-choice answering, many errors persist: early historical influence is carried by question-candidate states even after direct source access is blocked. Low-dimensional interventions further separate source-role information from answer-value information. Their effects peak at different depths, and changing the source-role signal does not eliminate the causal influence of competing values. On naturally occurring errors, strengthening the queried role and counteracting the historical value each improve answers; their joint intervention gives the greatest recovery. These findings support a failure of downstream evidence use beyond source identification alone: source-role information can influence a decision without exclusively controlling which historical values affect it. Reliable conversational memory therefore requires not only retention and retrieval, but also control over how retained information enters answer computation.

candidates.title: The Geometry of Ignorance: Detecting Suppressed Knowledge in LLMs through Activation Fragmentation
candidates.abstract: Evaluating whether a large language model (LLM) genuinely knows a concept remains a fundamental problem, since behavioral metrics can be fooled by suppression: a model that refuses to answer may still harbor recoverable knowledge. The framework measures the geometric coherence of \textit{anon-vectors}, the differences in hidden states between a concept-specific query and its anonymized paraphrase, and shows that genuine knowledge forms a tight, low-entropy cluster while ignorance forces geometric fragmentation. Across ten instruction-tuned LLMs from three model families, all fragmentation metrics reliably separate known from unknown concepts, and post-unlearning, fragmentation geometry correlates with adversarial recovery across four attack types and five unlearning algorithms, though the direction of that relationship is shown to depend on attack methodology. Furthermore, a layer-resolved analysis reveals that different adversarial mechanisms exploit this geometry at varying depths, with high attack-specific correlations that are invisible to behavioral evaluation. Together, these results constitute a single-phase, attack-free proxy for unlearning robustness that captures aspects of parametric knowledge inaccessible to output-level metrics. candidates.title: The Evolution Strategies Paradox: Better Models from Worse Perturbations
candidates.abstract: How is it possible for perturbation-based methods like Evolution Strategies (ES) to optimize billion-parameter large language models (LLMs)? Classical search methods are highly dependent on finding good candidates within generated populations. However, when using ES to fine-tune LLMs, a phenomenon can occur where all offspring models consistently perform worse than the parent model, yet during training, the parent model consistently improves. This paradox occurs across models, tasks, and even modalities. This paper characterizes the paradox, then examines how the local reward landscape and properties of the ES estimator contribute to it: in high-dimensional spaces, exploration leads to worse performance, yet still highlights good directions; aggregating those directions then allows for making local improvements. The result can be seen as a new optimization paradigm where a principled interaction of noise and curvature produces the paradox as a byproduct of effective optimization. These findings provide guidance for taking advantage of perturbation-based methods in LLM fine-tuning and in high-dimensional optimization in general.

candidates.title: The Agent Board: Kanban for Machines; Durable Coordination for Agents That Outlive the Conversation
candidates.abstract: Harnesses for large language models have converged on a single-threaded shape: one agent, one history, one machine, one sitting. That shape fails work that spans many agents, outlives any one model call, or waits on systems that are not agents. We describe the Agent Board, the coordination substrate in the Corvic harness. The board is a durable, shared table of semi-semantic tasks: a few exact fields the system routes on, and a free-form body that only language models read. Agents post tasks, watch tasks, and block on them, ending their turn and holding no process until a matching post wakes them. A system agent, the Board Keeper, acts as the interrupt handler for the board: it carries events from non-agent parts of the harness onto the board, matches them to waiting tasks by reading their prose, and allocates new agents for tasks that name a kind of agent rather than an instance. Loadable coordination policy kernels give statuses and roles meaning for a given pattern of work, without the board enforcing them. The design mirrors the kanban board a human team puts on a wall. We argue it is what persistent agent products such as Meta Muse, OpenAI dots and SpaceXAI Grok Bot need once an agent must wait, hand off work, or work with agents from another vendor. We view the board as an operating-system scheduler for agents and state where the analogy breaks. We separate what the mechanism guarantees from what it leaves to convention, and report a trace from a live board and three small simulated pilots. In the pilots, the wait cost of the board was flat in wait length while naive polling grew about 165-fold, but a plain external watcher was cheaper than the board. The Board Keeper matched prose waiters with no false wakes but missed 3.6 percent of real wakes.

candidates.title: Stabilizing On-Policy Targeted Guidance in Agentic Reinforcement Learning
candidates.abstract: Naive on-policy RL is often bottlenecked by the capabilities of the base model --- insufficient coverage can result in an inability to learn from certain rewards. At the same time, rewards in modern post-training systems often come from rich textual sources, e.g. judge models with a rubric of criteria. Can we utilize such structures to provide a rich directional signal that enables improving on otherwise difficult to optimize rewards? In this work, we examine a framework we refer to as targeted guidance that learns from per-turn textual feedback via an on-policy self-distillation objective. Our focus is not only on directly improving hard-to-optimize behaviors, but on how to do so throughout the training process without degrading baseline RL performance. Over a range of settings across an agentic multi-turn software engineering environment, we find success by combining targeted self-distillation with a per-criteria RL reward, and by limiting feedback to turns where the policy specifically fails. We further examine the design choices that lead to stable entropy and reduce oscillatory behavior throughout training.

candidates.title: Simulation-Based Basic Life Support Training: A QuasiExperimental Study Comparing Peyton’s Four-Step Approach with Traditional Teaching Among Undergraduate Medical Students
candidates.abstract: Background: Basic Life Support (BLS) competence is an essential requirement for medical graduates; however, traditional teaching may provide limited opportunities for active learning and structured practice. Peyton's FourStep Approach (PFSA) is a learner-centred method for teaching procedural skills, but evidence regarding its effectiveness in BLS skill acquisition and retention among undergraduate medical students in India remains limited. Objectives: To evaluate the effectiveness of Peyton's Four-Step Approach compared with Traditional Teaching Method (TTM) in improving immediate BLS skill performance and one-month skill retention among undergraduate medical students. Secondary objectives were to assess learner satisfaction and confidence with the two teaching methods. Methods: A quasi-experimental study was conducted among 100 third-year undergraduate medical students at GSL Medical College, Rajahmundry, Andhra Pradesh. Participants were non-randomly allocated into an experimental group receiving BLS training using Peyton's Four-Step Approach (n = 50) and a control group receiving Traditional Teaching Method (n = 50). BLS skills were assessed using a 15-item Objective Structured Clinical Examination (OSCE) checklist before training, immediately after training, and one month after the intervention. Student satisfaction and confidence were also assessed. Data were analysed using independent samples t-test and Chi-square test, with p < 0.05 considered statistically significant. Results: Baseline OSCE scores were comparable between the PFSA and TTM groups (5.82 ± 1.34 vs. 5.68 ± 1.41; p = 0.612). The PFSA group demonstrated significantly higher immediate post-training OSCE scores than the TTM group (12.46 ± 1.18 vs. 10.84 ± 1.47; mean difference: 1.62; p < 0.001). At one-month follow-up, skill retention remained significantly higher in the PFSA group (11.72 ± 1.29 vs. 9.63 ± 1.58; mean difference: 2.09; p < 0.001). Student satisfaction was higher in the PFSA group than in the TTM group (90% vs. 16%; χ² = 54.96; p < 0.001). Similarly, a greater proportion of students in the PFSA group reported confidence in performing BLS skills (88% vs. 10%; χ² = 30.43; p < 0.001). Conclusions: Peyton's Four-Step Approach was more effective than Traditional Teaching Method for improving immediate BLS skill performance and one-month skill retention among undergraduate medical students. The approach was also associated with greater student satisfaction and confidence. Incorporating structured, learnercentred approaches such as PFSA into undergraduate BLS training may enhance the acquisition and retention of essential resuscitation skills.

candidates.title: Self-Privileged Fine-Tuning
candidates.abstract: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) is a key component of language model post-training, enabling effective task adaptation and serving as an important foundation for subsequent reinforcement learning. Recent methods seek to improve SFT by introducing token-level weights into the training objective, where these weights are typically derived from a model's output distribution at each token position. To better understand how such weighting schemes affect SFT, we analyze their optimization objectives and theoretically characterize the target distributions they induce. Our analysis shows that dynamic weighting methods, such as Dynamic Fine-Tuning (DFT), induce a heavily sharpened distribution, whereas static weighting methods fit a target distribution proportional to the product of the data distribution and a frozen prior. These findings suggest that static weighting provides a more stable training target, while its effectiveness critically depends on the quality of the prior distribution. Building on this observation, we propose Self-Privileged Fine-Tuning (SPFT), which uses a frozen copy of the initial model conditioned on privileged information (such as ground truth for mathematical questions) as a prior to provide guidance for token-level weighting during fine-tuning. Through a Bayesian decomposition, we further show that SPFT reweights the standard static prior according to how informative each target token is for predicting the ground-truth outcome, thereby assigning larger weights to more predictive tokens. Experiments on mathematical reasoning and code generation show that SPFT improves over standard SFT and other baselines across the main settings.

candidates.title: Say Less, Mean Better: Training-Free Verbosity Control for Language Models
candidates.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) often generate responses longer than necessary, increasing inference latency and computational cost. While prompting can encourage conciseness, controlling output length without compromising response completeness remains challenging. Aggressive early stopping can reduce generation costs but risks terminating responses prematurely. We introduce MinimalLM, a training-free framework for reliable verbosity control that combines uncertainty-aware, length-dependent stop-token adjustment with structural completeness guardrails. MinimalLM separates the decision of when to stop from whether stopping is structurally appropriate, coordinating response-level instructions, decoding-time intervention, and completion checks without modifying model parameters or requiring auxiliary models. We evaluate MinimalLM across three open-source LLMs and 330 questions, producing 5,940 responses across baseline and ablation configurations. MinimalLM reduces generated tokens by 47.6%, accelerates individual responses by 19-68%, and eliminates structurally truncated outputs in the primary evaluation. Despite substantial token savings, it achieves an average quality score of 8.04/10, compared with 8.42/10 for unmodified models and 6.46/10 for length-matched truncation. Evaluations across diverse subject domains (such as healthcare, programming, law, and science) demonstrate robust efficiency gains, while ablations establish the complementary roles of decoding control and completeness constraints. Our findings highlight that efficient generation requires more than producing fewer tokens: it requires controlling when generation ends while preserving response integrity. MinimalLM offers a lightweight, training-free approach toward this goal.

candidates.title: SWAP-INR: Implicit Neural Representation with Switchable Attention Paths for Time-varying Multivariate Scientific Data Compression
candidates.abstract: Visualizing multivariate scientific simulation data is essential for understanding complex physical phenomena, yet the massive scale of such data imposes a severe storage bottleneck in high-performance computing environments. To address these limitations, we propose SWAP-INR, an architecture for high-fidelity compression of multivariate, time-varying simulation data. SWAP-INR introduces two key components: (1) The switchable attention path (SWAP) module explicitly models cross-variable interactions through a cross-variable attention layer, then routes each variable to an attention or non-attention path by a deterministic, loss-driven criterion, and prunes the inactive layers for structural compression. (2) The adaptability amplification SIREN (A2-SIREN) replaces rigid frequency scaling with channel-wise learnable modulation, adapting to heterogeneous physical features with negligible overhead. Combined with post-training 16-bit quantization, SWAP-INR achieves state-of-the-art performance on small modular reactor (SMR) datasets and remains competitive on public physics simulation datasets, while maintaining a constrained memory footprint. These results suggest that lightweight input structuring can change how closely different models’ outputs agree, and that it could serve as a low-cost, auditable preparation step for protocol-to-code tools built on free or open models. candidates.title: ReSI-Math: Exploring Recoverable Capability Frontiers for Efficient Reasoning Improvement
candidates.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has become an effective approach for improving mathematical reasoning in large language models. However, a fundamental question remains: when a model fails to solve a problem, does it truly lack the underlying capability? In this work, we reveal that direct failure does not necessarily imply inability. Some reasoning failures can be recovered by exploring the model's own trajectories, exposing a recoverable capability frontier: a policy-dependent region where solutions are not reliably generated through direct decoding but can be elicited through trajectory-level search. Based on this observation, we introduce ReSI-Math, a framework that explores recoverable capability frontiers and converts recovered capabilities into data-efficient RLVR supervision. ReSI-Math uses Self-Judge-guided evolutionary search to identify recoverable failures under a fixed policy and adaptively selects frontier problems for sequential RLVR as the policy evolves. On Qwen3-VL-8B, correct-incorrect trajectory crossover produces 272 verifier-confirmed correct offspring from 621 attempts (43.8%). candidates.title: Learnings and Pitfalls from AI-Assisted A/B Experimentation at Scale
candidates.abstract: A/B testing underpins product decisions by providing trustworthy, reproducible quantification of proposed changes' effects. Experiments are also operationally messy: diagnosing anomalies, debugging configurations, and conducting bespoke follow-up analyses require flexible reasoning and manual effort. These tasks let agents accelerate experimentation without replacing its deterministic statistical foundations. We report lessons from building and operating such an agent. Our central finding is that this tension is resolved not by making the model deterministic, but by bounding where its nondeterminism can reach; the model selects and sequences procedures, while deterministic code computes every quantity it reports. candidates.title: Knowingly Wrong: Training LLMs Against Their Own Beliefs can Induce Misalignment
candidates.abstract: Fine-tuning a large language model (LLM) on harmful data in a narrow domain, such as bad medical advice, can make it broadly misaligned. How realistic this risk is remains unclear, since models are very rarely fine-tuned on explicitly harmful data in practice. In this work, we show that fine-tuning on data the model believes to be false but that has no harmful content, can also induce broad misalignment. Across mathematics, trivia, cooking and sports, the more strongly the model disbelieves the answers it is trained on, the more misaligned it becomes. In mathematics, misaligned answers rise from 4% to over 60% as the training answers become more wrong, with little loss of general capability. After fine-tuning, the model states the wrong answers but its multiple-choice probabilities still prefer the true ones, which suggests that misalignment comes from this internal inconsistency. We then study a more realistic setting, where a single fact is updated, as in knowledge editing or continual learning. The same relationship holds and the more the model still believes the true fact after training on the false one, the more misaligned it becomes. When we frame the same false fact as part of a coherent story, the model comes to believe it more deeply and becomes less misaligned than when we instruct it to assert the false fact. This fluid analysis yields a $cμ$ priority rule, where the effective service rate $μ$ is jointly determined by computational speed, memory bandwidth, and memory capacity. We prove that this rule minimizes cumulative holding cost in the fluid model and, for a finite workload, also minimizes completion time and maximizes full-run output-token throughput. We then construct a feasible scheduling policy for the original finite system and prove that its scaled dynamics converge to the optimal fluid policy. Finally, experiments on a real LLM serving engine using an NVIDIA H800 show that practical implementations of the proposed priority rule substantially reduce average latency while maintaining high throughput relative to existing scheduling policies.

candidates.title: Amortized Nonlinear Variable Selection with Prior-Data Fitted Networks
candidates.abstract: Variable selection is an important task for interpreting potentially complex systems in fields such as biology, business, and sociology. The importance of variable selection has attracted considerable attention in statistics and machine learning. In this paper, we are mainly interested in model-agnostic variable selection for identifying variables that have general nonlinear dependence on the response. We propose MambaPFN, short for Model-Agnostic Markov BlAnket selection with Prior-data Fitted Networks, which is built upon the Transformer, a building block of many popular large language models. Specifically, we consider a functional-mapping perspective on variable-selection learning, in which the Transformer is treated as a learnable mapping from a dataset to its relevant variables. To learn this mapping, MambaPFN introduces three new components: (i) a faithful, rich, and scalable scheme for generating pretraining data, (ii) an objective that targets each variable's posterior inclusion probability, and (iii) a modified Transformer architecture tailored to variable selection. Once pretrained, MambaPFN is applied to new datasets without parameter updates. Empirically, MambaPFN achieves desirable variable-selection performance in simulation studies and exhibits a scaling law---more pretraining datasets and larger models can continuously improve its performance. Applied to a Facebook comments dataset, MambaPFN selects the fewest variables and achieves the highest computational efficiency and predictive performance, improving upon the best baselines by about 20%.

candidates.title: AgentAM: An AI Agent for Spatter- and Defect-Aware Process Optimization in Laser Powder Bed Fusion
candidates.abstract: Predictive models for laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) are rarely used on the shop floor because querying them requires programming and model-specific knowledge. We present AgentAM, a large language model (LLM) agent that gives process engineers natural-language access to CFD-trained surrogates of spatter and melt pool geometry for SS316L through the Model Context Protocol (MCP). Polynomial surrogates trained on 279 single-track simulations predict melt pool dimensions ($R^2 \geq 0.95$) and spatter volume ($R^2 = 0.83$ on test data) at any power-velocity point in the trained range, and geometric criteria assign each point a geometry-derived defect regime (keyhole, lack of fusion, balling or stable) that matches the regime obtained from the simulated geometry in 93.4% of tracks under cross-validation. The agent selects and parameterizes tools for prediction, process-window scans and constrained optimization. Minimum-spatter optima often sat within 10 $μ$m of the lack-of-fusion boundary; a margin-aware optimizer moved them away from all thresholds and raised the estimated probability of remaining classified Good from 0.94 to 1.00 under an assumed 2% process drift, and from 0.72 to 0.91 when jointly sampled cross-validated geometry residuals were added. About 40-50 well-spread simulations sufficed to reproduce the defect map. To evaluate the agent layer, we introduce a 145-prompt benchmark scored against direct tool calls, plus eight prompts (40 runs) on margin-aware requests. Over the 725 runs of the main benchmark the agent passed the intended inputs in 98.5% of parsing prompts, reported the scored spatter values and defect classes faithfully and met every stated constraint in the 65 feasible optimization runs, within a median 1.0% of the brute-force optimum.

candidates.title: Adversarial Speculative Reasoning Improves Long Horizon Agents
candidates.abstract: Speculative decoding has been treated purely as a systems optimization that speeds up large language model decoding without changing the model behavior. Under this view, the growing effort to train better draft models has been focused solely on acceptance rate. We argue that this view does not hold true for long-horizon agent reasoning. Measuring frontier open-weight models on complex agentic tasks with different speculative decoding approaches, we found that numerical noise grows within verification windows, and the draft acceptance results of the thinking process can change the output distribution of the model after 30 steps, thus noticeably influencing the reasoning accuracy of long-horizon agents in random directions. In this work, we improve the reasoning capability of target models by controlling such noise. While we cannot change the overall token distribution verified by the target model, we can encode critical reasoning with highest precision by training the draft model to be rejected. We identify these points in agent traces and train the draft model to favor adversarial preference. At inference the trained draft and the target part ways precisely at these decision points, verification restarts, so that critical thinking tokens are sampled from the target model and encoded under its least noisy conditions. This approach makes critical reasoning better indexed and more durable over a long horizon. On complex agentic coding benchmarks, our approach raises end-to-end success rate with no change to the target model or its output distribution. Our results recast the speculative decoding mechanism from a pure accelerator into an active allocator for context precision that improves the accuracy of long-horizon agents by training 0.06% to 0.28% of hosted parameters.

candidates.title: ALBI: LLM-Guided Inductive Logic Programming via Iterative Generate-Test-Constrain Refineme
candidates.abstract: We introduce ALBI (Agent for Learning By Induction), a neuro-symbolic ILP framework that replaces the ASP-based hypothesis generator in the Learning from Failures (LFF) paradigm with a Large Language Model (LLM), while retaining SWI-Prolog as a formal verifier. ALBI implements an iterative generate-test-constrain loop: the LLM proposes candidate hypotheses from structured prompts; Prolog tests each candidate; and diagnostic feedback drives refinement. We further introduce semantic anonymization, a metamorphic testing methodology, to distinguish structural symbolic induction from surface-level pattern matching on predicate names. Experiments on 30 standard ILP benchmarks show that ALBI achieves 100% success across three frontier LLMs (Gemini 3.1 Pro, GPT 5.4 Pro, Claude Opus 4.6), matching Popper while requiring only 1.4-1.7 iterations on average. Under anonymization, all models maintain 100% success with a moderate iteration increase (1.36-1.67 times), providing evidence of robust symbolic reasoning.

candidates.title: Follow the Features: SAE Feature-Guided Data-Efficient Instruction-Tuning of Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Selecting small, effective instruction-tuning datasets requires identifying which aspects of the original data to retain. We introduce Follow the Features (FtF), a data-selection method that uses sparse autoencoder (SAE) features to characterize training data and guide subset construction. FtF ranks features using dataset-level activation statistics, scores samples by their expression of highly ranked features, and incorporates feature resampling to encourage diversity. The LLM-SAE pair used for selection is independent of the model being fine-tuned, enabling reuse across target models. We evaluate FtF on two model-dataset settings at a training budget of 100 samples with a fixed sequence length of 256 tokens. FtF achieves performance competitive with GRAPE and S2L, with relative rankings varying across settings. On Qwen 3 8B trained on Alpaca, FtF exceeds full-dataset training by 1.59 percentage points in the harmonic mean of an AlpacaEval-based win rate and Open LLM Leaderboard performance, although full-dataset training retains a higher Leaderboard score. These results support SAE feature statistics as a useful signal for data-efficient instruction tuning.
